title: Cost & Latency Optimization
summary: The real-world engineering trade-offs that separate a demo from a production AI feature.

slides.markdown:
A demo calls the biggest model with a long prompt and nobody notices the bill. A production feature runs that same call millions of times a day — at that point, token cost and latency stop being an afterthought and become a first-class design constraint.

- **Cost** — every token in and out has a price; prompt design is a cost decision.
- **Latency** — users notice both time-to-first-token and total response time.
- The levers: routing, caching, smaller/quantized models, and streaming.

slides.subTitle: Prompt design is also a cost decision
slides.markdown:
Most hosted LLM APIs charge per token, input and output separately, often with output tokens priced higher than input. This means a bloated system prompt, unnecessary few-shot examples, or an overly long retrieved context isn't just a latency problem — it's a **recurring cost multiplied by every single call**, forever, until someone trims it.

The practical habit: measure token count per request the same way you'd measure a hot-path database query — it's a cost center, and small savings compound at scale.

slides.subTitle: Cheap model for easy cases, expensive for hard ones
slides.markdown:
**Model routing** sends each request to the cheapest model that can handle it: a small, fast, inexpensive model classifies or attempts the request first, and only genuinely hard or ambiguous cases escalate to a larger, more expensive model. Since most real-world requests are the "easy" majority, this can cut average cost dramatically while preserving quality on the hard tail.

The routing decision itself needs to be cheap and reliable — a bad router that sends easy cases to the expensive model (wasting money) or hard cases to the cheap one (hurting quality) undermines the whole point.

slides.subTitle: Caching and batching
slides.markdown:
Two techniques cut wasted calls: **caching** (exact-match or semantic — see [LLM App Architecture](llm-app-architecture)) skips the model when a sufficiently similar request was already answered. **Batching** groups multiple requests into one inference call where hardware allows, improving throughput and lowering per-request cost, at the cost of a small added delay while requests accumulate.

Batching matters most for self-hosted or fine-tuned serving, where you control the inference stack directly; it's largely invisible when calling a hosted API.

slides.subTitle: Quantization and distillation at a glance
slides.markdown:
**Quantization** reduces the numeric precision of a model's weights (16-bit down to 8-bit or 4-bit), shrinking memory footprint and speeding inference with usually small, controllable quality loss. **Distillation** trains a smaller "student" model to mimic a larger "teacher's" outputs, capturing most of its capability in a fraction of the parameters.

Both serve cheaper without changing what the model does — quantization compresses an existing model, distillation trains a new, smaller one to imitate it.

slides.subTitle: Streaming and partial responses
slides.markdown:
Total cost and total generation time don't shrink just because a response streams — but **perceived** latency does, since the user starts reading within a few hundred milliseconds instead of waiting for the full answer. For structured output, partial JSON parsing lets a UI progressively fill in fields as they complete, rather than blocking on the entire response.

This is a genuinely different lever from the cost-reduction techniques above — it's about *user experience under a fixed cost*, not reducing the underlying compute or spend.

slides.subTitle: Latency-sensitive vs throughput-sensitive
slides.markdown:
| | Chat (latency-sensitive) | Batch (throughput-sensitive) |
|---|---|---|
| Priority | Fast first token, low per-request latency | Maximum requests processed per dollar/hour |
| Batching | Limited — waiting hurts perceived speed | Aggressive — no user is waiting live |
| Model choice | Smaller/faster models, or routing | Can afford larger models if throughput math still works |
| Caching value | High — repeated similar questions | Lower — often unique inputs per record |

**How to decide:** optimize chat-style workloads for time-to-first-token and routing; optimize batch/offline workloads for cost-per-unit-of-work, since nothing is waiting on any single response.
